en: In the thirty-first [chapter], however, there are the dialogues between Hari and the gopīs for the sake of the rāsa dance,
as well as his disappearance during the excitement of the rāsa.
Victorious is the Lord of Śrī, the ornament of the circle of cowherd maidens, who destroys the pride of Kāmadeva— the pride which had grown through his conquest of Brahmā and the other gods.
Śrī Śuka said:
Even the Blessed One, beholding those nights when the mallikā jasmine was in full bloom in autumn,
set his mind upon sporting, having resorted to his yogic power (yogamāyā).

[*1] Although autumn lacks the status of being the cause for the blooming of jasmine flowers, by describing it as the cause, its novelty is suggested; and by that, the blossoming of all flowers is implied.
But is this not the opposite?
For from the pleasure of another's wife, there is the perception of being a conqueror of Kandarpa (the God of Love).
It is not so; for [the texts state]: "He relied upon his yogic power," "Though delighting in the Self, he took pleasure [in the world]," and "He is the direct destroyer of the God of Love."
Because of the declaration of His absolute sovereignty in such passages as, "He who has restrained all sexual passion within Himself," and so forth;
therefore, the truth is simply this: the imitation of the *rāsa* pastimes is for the purpose of proclaiming His victory over desire.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that this work of five chapters, though appearing under the guise of erotic discourse, is specifically intent upon renunciation;
the meaning is that those nights were promised to them by the words: "The women have gone to Vraja, but these nights you shall enjoy with me, for they are already accomplished."
Then the moon, the lord of stars, rose up, anointing the face of the eastern quarter with his most auspicious, ruddy rays;
he appeared like a beloved long-sighted lover who comes to wipe away the sorrows of his beloved among the people.
Then, at that very moment, for the sake of perceiving that [face], the moon, the king of stars, rose;
what was it doing?
It was as if it were anointing with red saffron the face of its beloved, which had been long desired to behold.

Likewise, the face of the eastern quarter [is being treated] by the rays— meaning the beams— which are most peaceful and most pleasant, as he, the well-known king of stars (the moon), anoints it with a ruddy glow at sunrise, that is, makes it red.
Likewise, he cleansed—that is, removed—the afflictions of heat and exhaustion of the people, that is, of the subjects.
Beholding the full-orbed moon, which resembled the face of Lakṣmī and was as red as fresh saffron,
and seeing the forest colored by its tender rays, he sang a sweet song that captivated the hearts of beautiful-eyed women.
*Kumudvantam* means one who possesses *kumuda*, that is, a blooming white water-lily (*kumut*).
*Akhaṇḍamaṇḍalam* means one whose orb is not fragmented. *Ramānanābham* means one whose luster is like the splendor of the face of Ramā.
Having seen the moon thus, red like fresh saffron,
and likewise having seen the forest colored by its tender rays (gobhiḥ), he sang— indeed, he chanted— sweetly and melodiously.
How?
Of those women whose glances were beautiful and captivating, [he gazed] in a manner that was enchanting to them.
Having heard that song which increases passion, the women of Vraja, their minds captivated by Kṛṣṇa,
went to where their beloved was— unobserved in their efforts and with earrings swaying from their haste.
Those women, who had made an unobserved and undisclosed effort toward one another to ensure they would not become rivals,
arrived here and there by way of the sound of singing;
their earrings were trembling and swaying with speed and momentum.
Although "they went" (*jagmuḥ*) should have been said, the expression "they came" (*ājagmuḥ*) is used because Śuka perceived his own presence in the vicinity of Kṛṣṇa.
Some, filled with longing, went forth abandoning their milking;
others, having set the milk on the fire, departed without removing the *saṃyāva* from the oven.
The word *aparāḥ* (others) connects with both what precedes and what follows.

By hearing the sound indicating Śrī Kṛṣṇa, those whose minds were inclined toward Him departed, as if manifesting the immediate cessation of activities pertaining to the three goals of life (*traivargika-karma*) for those whose hearts were thus focused; they went forth, abandoning their work half-finished.
This is expressed by the words "milking" (*duhantyaḥ*).
Some women, having placed the milk in a pot upon the hearth, departed without waiting for it to boil;
others left the wheat-flour cakes and parched grain already cooked, without having removed them from the fire or taken them down.
Some were anointing themselves, others were wiping away [tears], and some were applying collyrium to their eyes;
with their garments and ornaments disarrayed, some went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
"Smearing" means applying body ointments;
"others wiping" means performing tasks such as massaging the limbs.
To show that for the sake of pleasing Kṛṣṇa, any action performed with a mind intent upon Him bears fruit even if done otherwise than prescribed, he says: "with [limbs] crossed," and so forth.
Those whose garments and ornaments had undergone a reversal of position—both in their placement and their nature—due to being held upside down.
Though restrained by their husbands, fathers, brothers, and kinsmen,
they did not turn back, being deluded and having had their hearts stolen away by Govinda.
And it is said—“those [obstacles], being warded off”—because obstacles do not prevail over those whose minds are drawn away by the Dark One (Kṛṣṇa).
Some gopīs who had gone inside the house and were unable to find a way out remained with their eyes closed, absorbed in meditation upon Kṛṣṇa.
Their eyes are sealed,
or else they are those whose eyes are closed and who possess no other knowledge;
they are those by whom no exit has been found.
The meaning is that those who were already engaged in the cultivation of that [meditation] previously would then meditate upon it even more intensely.
Their impurities were shaken off by the intense suffering of separation from their beloved Duḥsaha;
their auspicious merits were exhausted through the bliss of embracing Acyuta, attained via meditative absorption.
Even by uniting with that very Supreme Self through the thought of him as a lover,
they immediately cast off their bodies composed of the *guṇas*, their bonds being utterly destroyed.

Furthermore, he explains in two verses how, having thus attained that Supreme Self, Kṛṣṇa, through meditation, they abandoned their bodies composed of the *guṇas*, beginning with the words "duḥsaha" (unbearable). Now, one might object: "How could they abandon them? For they lacked knowledge of him as the Supreme Self. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "even with the thought of him as a lover (*jāra*).
Indeed, the inherent power of a reality does not depend upon the intellect.

The sense is that even though they thought otherwise, it was as if they had drunk nectar. Now, one might ask: "Even so, while the bondage of *prārabdha* karma still exists, how could they abandon it? To this he says: "Their bonds were instantly destroyed. Again, one might ask: "How can *prārabdha* karma be exhausted without experience? It is only through experience that it is exhausted; how then is it said to be 'instantly' exhausted? To this he says: "Unbearable."
The meaning is that their impurities (*aśubha*) have been shaken off by the intense torment caused by that unbearable separation from their beloved;
thus, their evil has been exhausted through the experience of the supreme suffering of not attaining him.

Likewise, their auspicious merit (*maṅgala*), which is a bond of *puṇya*, has been exhausted through that bliss (*nirvṛti*)—the enjoyment of supreme happiness—which they attained through the embrace of the Infallible One (*acyuta*) via meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Therefore, because they attained the Supreme Self through meditation, their karma was completely exhausted by the pleasure and pain experienced at that time, and they abandoned the body composed of the gunas.

[*6] Here, by the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even with the intent to kill [him], for Hari," the censurability of such a thought is suggested—just as in the case of "even with the notion that he was a lover"—and yet, through the majesty of the subject matter, its extreme excellence is implied.
[*7] By the statement "they abandoned their bodies composed of qualities" (*guṇamaya*), it is suggested that they attained Him in His spiritual body (*cinmaya-deha*) in Goloka and other realms.
The King said:
O Sage, they know Kṛṣṇa as the supreme beloved, but not as Brahman;
for how could there be a cessation of the flow of the *guṇas* for those whose intellects are fixed upon the *guṇas*?

Therefore, for those whose intellects are fixed on His qualities—those whose love consists solely in being bound to the qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—is there a cessation of the flow of those qualities, and a cessation of that spiritual form which is the locus of a succession of spiritual qualities? How could this be liberation by union (*sāyujya-mukti*), as it is for those who worship Brahman?

[Objection: But surely, just as there is no liberation from worshipping one's husband, sons, and so forth—even though they are in reality Brahman—because of the absence of such realization; so too [is it here].

In this way, one might raise the doubt: "Since Kṛṣṇa is also [an object of worldly perception], how can association with him—given the absence of the realization that he is Brahman—be a cause for liberation? To this, it is said: "They know Kṛṣṇa...
He is the supreme, absolute, beautiful, and desirable one.
Śrī Śuka said:
This was told to you previously—how even the King of Cedi attained perfection despite being an enemy of Hṛṣīkeśa; how much more so those who are dear to Adhokṣaja!
He refutes [the objection] with the words "it has been said.
The meaning is this: while the nature of Brahman is veiled in living beings, it is not veiled in Kṛṣṇa because He is Hṛṣīkeśa; therefore, there is no dependence on the intellect in that case.
O King, for the sake of the supreme welfare of men, there is the manifestation of the Blessed One—
who is imperishable, immeasurable, devoid of qualities, yet whose very self consists of the qualities.
[9] Of that which is immeasurable and unlimited.
Now, one might ask: "How can the embodied soul be unobstructed? To this he says: "Of men.
[It belongs to Him who is] the self of the qualities, the controller of the qualities.
The meaning is that since the manifestation of the Blessed One is of such a nature, it is not appropriate to speak of a similarity to a physical body in this context.
Those who constantly direct desire, anger, fear, affection, a sense of oneness, and even friendship toward Hari indeed attain identity with Him.
The reading is "vidadhate.
This refers to becoming absorbed in that [the Lord], which includes liberation such as *sāyujya* (union) and *sārūpya* (similarity of form), as well as the constant manifestation of Him alone.
Therefore, he says "kāmam" (even if), meaning that attachment to Him by any means whatsoever is the cause of liberation.
Aikya means relationship;
sauhṛda means devotion.
And you should not feel such astonishment toward the unborn Blessed One,
Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Lords of Yoga, for by him this [world] is liberated.
And this is not too great a burden for the Blessed One; thus he says, "Nor is it so," because even these stationary beings and others are liberated through Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing those women of Vraja approaching his presence, the Blessed One,
the best among speakers, spoke, enchanting them with his elegant words.
He states what is introduced [in the verse]: "Having seen them," meaning by means of the charms of speech, that is, the playful expressions of speech.

[*12] Indicating that such a question and its elaborate response on the part of [the sages] would be inappropriate because it would obstruct the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) during the course of this erotic play (*rāsalīlā*), the Blessed Lord himself, out of longing, introduces the conversation: "Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones! What pleasing thing may I do for you?"
Is all well with Vraja? Tell me the reason for your coming.
Seeing them all arrive in a state of agitation, she spoke as if with fear: "Of Vraja... (BhP 10.29.18).
"This night is terrible in form and frequented by fierce creatures;
depart for Vraja, O slender-waisted women—you must not remain here."
Alternatively, she is "non-terrible" (*aghorarūpā*) because darkness is dispelled by the rising of the moon;
thus, due to the moonlight making it almost like day, she is frequented by non-terrible beings such as bees, cuckoos, and the like.
Or else, she is "frequented by me," who possess a "terrible" (*ghoram*) being—that is, a strength—that produces fear in the wicked.
Therefore, by all means, do not go to Vraja;
the *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*).
Let them not search for you in this very manner hereafter.
The phrase "Do not go," and so forth, should be applied here.
Observing a gentle smile born of bashfulness, he said: "This is the night."
Your mothers, fathers, sons, brothers, and husbands are searching for you, not seeing you; do not feel anxiety for your kinsmen.
Furthermore, regarding the word "mothers":
they search and seek [for you]. The meaning is: "Do not cause distress or hardship for your kinsmen; do not do so. (BhPC 10.29.20)
The forest was seen in full bloom, colored by the rays of the full moon,
beautified by the play of the Yamunā breeze that caused the tree sprouts to tremble.
Looking away with a slight touch of amorous indignation, she replied, "It has been seen.
It was colored by the rays of the lord of the night, the full moon;
it was beautified by the trembling sprouts of the trees, which were shaken by the playful, slow movement—the grace—of the breeze that touches the Yamunā.
Therefore, go to the cow-pen without delay; as virtuous wives, serve your husbands. The calves and the young children are crying; give them their drink and milk the cows.
O truthful ones, O you who are true!
Or rather, you have come here with your intentions restrained by affection for me; for it is only natural that living beings find pleasure in me.
He replies to those whose eyes are agitated by impetuosity with the words "Alternatively" (*athavā*). "With restrained intentions" means having their minds brought under control.
"Appropriate" (*upapanna*) means logical (*yukta*).
They are pleased; they become joyful.
For women, the highest duty is indeed the sincere service of their husband,
as well as that of his kinsmen and the nurturing of their offspring, O auspicious ladies.
He turns [the disciple] away by demonstrating the fear of both the seen and the unseen, through the three verses beginning with "Of the master," and so forth.
For a woman of noble family, an extramarital affair is everywhere condemned; it leads away from heaven, brings ill repute, is trivial, difficult, fraught with danger, and universally despised.
Phalgu means worthless; kṛcchra means difficult to accomplish;
aupapattyam refers to the pleasure of a paramour.
Devotion toward me arises from hearing, seeing, meditating, and chanting my praises;
it does not arise in the same way through physical proximity. Therefore, return to your homes.
Furthermore, [it is said]: "and from hearing."
Lowering their faces, drying the bimba-like lips with their sighs, scratching the earth with their feet,
and wiping the saffron from their breasts with tears that served as ink, they stood silent, burdened by a weight of immense sorrow.
He describes the state of those who have fallen into anxiety with the word "having done so" (*kṛtvā*).
Having cast their faces downward— faces whose lips, resembling *bimba* fruits, were drying from the breath rising out of grief— and likewise scratching the earth with their thumbs,
they stood silent, washing away the saffron on their breasts with tears stained by collyrium.
Those women for whom the burden of manifold suffering is a heavy load.
To Kṛṣṇa, who was speaking as if he were someone other than their dearest friend, those devoted women— having renounced all desires for his sake—
wiped their eyes, which were impaired by weeping, and spoke with voices somewhat faltering from agitation.
Furthermore, regarding the words "What is most dear?":
with voices faltering due to some degree of agitation and the onset of anger, they spoke;
the cause of that agitation is expressed by the phrase beginning with "What is most dear? and so forth.
He spoke as if he were someone utterly disliked, and he rejected [the request].
The gopīs said:

"O All-pervading Lord, you ought not speak such cruel words. Having abandoned all sense-objects, we have taken refuge at the soles of your feet; O one difficult to restrain, favor us, your devotees! Do not abandon us, just as the Original Person, the God, favors those seeking liberation."
"O cruel and harsh one! O you who are difficult to restrain and act according to your own whims!
You should favor us, your devotees who have served at the soles of your feet; do not abandon us! // BhPC 10.29.31 //
"O dear one, you who know the dharma have said that for women, devotion to husband, children, and friends is their own duty.
Let it be so; yet, since you are the Lord, the very ground of instruction, you are indeed the dearest friend and the very self of all embodied beings."
Or, it may mean "one whose self is charming and captivating.

Furthermore, as for what you said—beginning with "husband, children," etc.—claiming that I am a knower of dharma, this is merely said in jest; let such [misguided] instructions remain only within your own domain.
The reason for [the Veda] being the basis of instruction is "the Lord" (īśa);
the sense is that, through the *vividiṣā* passage, it is understood that all instructions have the Lord as their ultimate purpose.
The reason for His being the Lord is: "Indeed, you are the Self."

For since the Self alone is the master and enjoyer of everything that is to be enjoyed, you alone are our dearest kinsman; thus, the duty that ought to be performed toward all kinsmen should reside in you alone—this is the meaning.

Alternatively, while you stand in the place or position of the instructors of dharma as the teacher of dharma, and while we are desirous of knowing dharma, what has been spoken by you, the knower of dharma, is indeed so; for you are not merely an instructor of dharma, but you are the Self.
Alternatively, as for what was said regarding that person who is the object of this instruction: let it be so for him;
but since You, the Lord, are the Master, how could it not be so for You? This is the meaning.

Since you are the Self of embodied beings and the very form of the fruit [of their actions], or rather, as it has been said, "Service to husbands and so forth is dharma"—let this be so in your case alone.
Why? Because...
"In the station of instruction" means in the station or foundation of the husband and others who are taught as those to be served. Why? Because "he is the Lord";
for no one such as a husband, son, or the like exists without the Lord as their foundation.
The rest is the same.
Enough with excessive detail. //BhPC_10,29.32//
For the wise find delight in their own self, which is eternally dear; what use have they for husbands, sons, and the like, who bring only suffering?
Therefore, be gracious to us, O Supreme Lord; O Lotus-eyed One, do not cut short the hope that we have long cherished in you.
[*15] Within the self, in the self.
[*16] The reading is "O Lord of the Boon-granters.
[*17] The reading is "he should cut off hope."
In this context, the word "bhavān" (you) is to be supplied, or there is a Vedic transposition of the person.
Strengthening this by means of the conduct of the virtuous, they pray: "May you do so."
They are virtuous and skilled in the treatises.
And thus says the scripture: "What shall we do with offspring, for us this self and this world [are already ours]? (BhPC 10.29.33)
Your mind has been captivated by happiness in the home, such that it finds no pleasure even in our domestic duties;
your feet do not stir from the base of your own feet—how then shall we go to Vraja, or what indeed shall we do?
Furthermore, they say that what was stated—"return"—is impossible, because you yourself have stolen away our minds and so forth; thus they say: "The mind.
That mind of ours which for so long a time has been enjoying itself at home in comfort—that has been stolen by you.
Even those two hands that attend to household chores—
[you have made them] thus by means of your blissful self.

O friend, sprinkle with the vessel of the nectar of your lower lip the fire of love in my heart, which is fanned by your smiles, glances, and sweet songs; otherwise, our bodies consumed by the fire born of separation, we shall, through meditation, attain the state of your feet.
Therefore, O dear Kṛṣṇa,
quench with Your glance accompanied by a smile and Your sweet song that fire of desire born within our hearts through the nectar of Your lips;
otherwise, we shall first become a single fire born of separation, and with that fire, having consumed our bodies like yogins, we shall attain Your state, reaching Your presence through meditation.

O lotus-eyed one, whenever we touched the sole of your foot—which at times is granted a moment’s rest even to the beloved of the forest-dwellers—O dear one, from that time forth we have not been able to stand in the presence of another, for we are delighted by you. Alas! We are no longer capable of remaining in the company of others.
If it is argued that they should approach their own husbands and sprinkle this fire [with water], to that they reply with the word "yarhi" (when).
[This occurs] when an occasion, a festival, or an opportunity has been granted by Ramā (Lakṣmī);
and even then, only at certain times, not always.
O you for whom forest-dwellers are dear,

because of that love for forest-folk, whenever we touched you anywhere in the forest and were delighted and gladdened by you there, from that time on we have not been able to remain even in the presence of others.
The meaning is that those things do not please them because they are empty.
Lakṣmī desired the dust of Your lotus feet even after she had obtained a place upon Your chest, which is cherished by Your servants;
for the sake of obtaining even a glance from You, other gods exert themselves—just like her, we too have taken refuge in the dust of Your feet.

They say that the good fortune of Your feet is exceedingly wonderful: "Śrī," though she has obtained a place upon Your chest free from rivalry, still yearns for the dust of Your lotus feet along with her rival Tulasī.
The phrase "adored by all Your servants" expresses the excellence of that good fortune.

For the sake of beholding her, Śrī herself exerts effort through the austerities of others, such as Brahmā and the rest, with the thought, "Look upon me"; we too have likewise sought refuge in that *rajas*.
Thus [ends verse 37].
Therefore, be gracious to us, O Destroyer of Sins; having abandoned our homes, we have come to the soles of Your feet, longing for Your service.
O Ornament of Men, grant the state of servitude to those whose souls are scorched by the intense passion born from gazing upon Your beautiful smile.
O destroyer of sin and remover of suffering!
We, whose only hope lies in serving and worshipping you, have abandoned our homes— leaving behind our wives— and have arrived like yogis,
our hearts scorched by the intense passion ignited by the sight of your beautiful smile and playful glances.
O jewel among men,
grant me your service.
Beholding your face veiled by your curls, your cheeks radiant with the beauty of earrings, your lips like nectar, your smiling glance,
your pair of staff-like arms granting fearlessness, and your chest— the sole beloved of the Goddess Śrī— we shall become your handmaidens.
[*18] In the negative interpretation (*niṣedhapakṣe*), the word division is *vṛjinārda na* (not from the source of sin);
the construction is: "We have not arrived [here] after abandoning our homes and so forth. [*19] The word division is *śriyaḥ ekaramaṇam* (the sole delight of Fortune).
The *sandhi* is archaic (*ārṣa*).
In the context of the negative interpretation, the rhetorical question "Shall we become slaves? implies "Certainly not.
[An objection is raised: "But why is slavery being requested after abandoning the ownership of one's home? To this they reply: "He will look [at us]. (*vīkṣyati*)

Having beheld your face—its surface covered by locks of hair and its cheeks possessing the splendor of two earrings; and having beheld that pair of staff-like arms which grant fearlessness, as well as your chest which possesses nectar upon its lower lip; and having beheld [the Lord] who is the sole lover, the producer of delight through his beauty—the maidservants... [became filled with devotion].
"May we indeed become thus."
What woman in the three worlds, whose noble conduct has been deluded by your sweet-toned, long-sustained resonance, would not tremble?
For even the cows, the twice-born, the trees, and the deer displayed horripilation upon beholding this form, the very fortune of the three worlds.
The reading is “*padāyataveṇugītasaṃmohitā*.
In the context of the prohibitive position (*niṣedhapakṣe*), the construction is: “Out of fear of violating the conduct of the noble ones (*āryacarita*), what woman would not flee?
Now, it was indeed stated that [engaging in] illicit sexual union is loathsome.
Regarding this, they ask: "Which woman?

O dear Kṛṣṇa, [she is one who possesses] that which is long and drawn out (*āyatam*), consisting of melodious words (*kalāni padāni*) and modulated by the distinctions of melodic intonation (*mūrcchita-svarālāpa-bheda*).

In another reading [*23], [it says]: "What woman of noble conduct would not be moved from her own duty by that flute-song consisting of the nectar of beautiful words, by which even men have been deluded and shaken? Moreover, it is the fortune of the three worlds," because they bore it, they maintained it.
The sense is: even by merely hearing a word that reveals you, the abandonment of one's own dharma is appropriate; how much more so, then, through direct experience of you?
"Deluded by the nectar-like flute-song of Kala-padā,
you have clearly been born as a god who removes the fear and suffering of Vraja, just like the Primordial Person who protects the world of the gods.
Therefore, O kinsman of the distressed, place your lotus-hand upon the burning breasts and the heads of us, your maidservants."

The reading is "vrajajanārtiharaḥ" (the remover of the suffering of the people of Vraja). In the sense of prohibition, it means: "Do not place your hand even upon the heads of your maidservants; do not set it there. This is clear and certain. (BhP 10.29.41)
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard their lamentation, the Lord of the masters of yoga,
though finding delight in the Self alone, smiled compassionately and brought joy to the gopīs.
*Viklavitaṃ* means lamentation due to helplessness;
he *arīramat*, that is, he caused the cowherd girls to rejoice.
Accompanied by those women of noble conduct, whose faces blossomed at the sight of their beloved,
the Imperishable One shone like the moon surrounded by stars, his noble smile possessing the luster of jasmine flowers.
He whose radiance is like the *kunda* flower amidst those [women] whose faces bloom at the sight of their beloved, and who possesses a smile as noble as the twice-born [teeth],
is the deer-marked moon.
By stretching out his arms for embraces, by the seizing of their thighs, waist-knots, and breasts, by playful strikes with his fingernails,
by jesting, glances, and laughter, he delighted the beauties of Vraja while enkindling the Lord of Love within them.
Extending his arms, embracing, touching and stroking their hands and other limbs, jesting and laughing, scratching them with his fingernails,
and through playful dalliance and glances, he delighted them by fully inflaming their passion.
Thus, having received honors from the high-souled Lord Kṛṣṇa,
those proud women considered themselves preeminent among all women on earth.
From the Great-Souled One whose mind is liberated.
Seeing their intoxication with that good fortune and their pride, Keśava vanished right there for the sake of their pacification and grace.
By His auspiciousness, He subdues intoxication— which is lack of self-control—
and pride— which is arrogance.
He is Keśava because He brings under His control both *ka* (the individual soul) and *īśa* (the presiding deity).
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the first half of the tenth book of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the commentary *Bhāvārthadīpikā*.
In the thirtieth [chapter], Kṛṣṇa is sought by the gopīs, who, tormented by the pain of separation,
wander incessantly through forest after forest like those intoxicated.
Śrī Śuka said:
When the Blessed One had suddenly vanished, the women of Vraja,
not seeing him, were tormented like female elephants separated from their leader.
Not speaking, not seeing.
With their gait, amorous glances, playful smiles, and sidelong looks; with their charming conversation and graceful movements;
the women, their hearts captivated, then assumed those various gestures characteristic of the Lord of Ramā.
By their gait, their affectionate smiles, their graceful glances— those looks full of charm— and by those delightful conversations, pastimes, sports, amorous gestures,
and other such playful charms, the hearts of those women were captivated and drawn away by these very qualities of the Lord of Ramā, beginning with His gait.
Therefore, those whose very self was that [child] took up his various movements and played by imitating him.

In their movements, smiles, glances, speech, and other gestures, these beloved women— whose very forms were reflected in those of their beloved and who were absorbed in the playful sports of Kṛṣṇa— manifested themselves as being one with him, declaring, "I am he."
Moreover, regarding the phrase "gatismitāḥ": those whose forms (mūrtayaḥ) are established in—that is, permeated by—the gait and other qualities of their beloved;
therefore, they possess the playful movements and amorous sports (vihāravibhramāḥ) that are the very play and grace of Kṛṣṇa himself.
"I am indeed Kṛṣṇa," they said to one another.
Singing loudly about him alone, they wandered together from forest to forest like madmen;
they questioned the lords of the forest regarding the Person who dwells within all beings, both internally and externally, like the space within the sky.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "singing":
while going from forest to forest, they searched—that is, they sought them out.
He describes their state as being like that of madmen: they questioned the lords of the forest (the trees).
"The Person who exists within beings, in their midst, and also exists outside of them. //BhPC_10,30.4//
"O Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha, have you seen him? Has the son of Nanda gone away, having stolen our hearts with his loving smiles and glances?"

He elaborates upon this in nine verses: therein, with the hope that they might see [the thief] because of their greatness, they ask about the *aśvattha* tree and others, saying, "Was he seen?"—having stolen our hearts with glances shimmering with love and laughter, he has gone away like a thief; was he seen by you? || BhPC 10.30.5 ||
I hope that the Kurabaka, Aśoka, Nāga, Punnāga, and Campaka trees here have had their pride humbled by the smiles of Rāma’s younger brother, who puts an end to the haughtiness of proud women.
The reading is "gataḥ" (gone).
[The gods], seeing that the great ones have been of much benefit with their own flowers, ask the *kurabaka* trees and others: "Kaccit...
O *kurabaka* trees and so forth!
"Has he, whose smile removes all pride, gone from here? Have you perhaps seen him?"
O auspicious Tulasī, beloved of Govinda’s feet,
have you seen Acyuta, who is so exceedingly dear to you, together with the swarms of bees?
"Carrying you along with the swarms of bees, he is exceedingly dear to you; what did he see? she asked.
O Mālatī, Mallikā, Jātī, and Yūthikā, have you been seen?
Has Mādhava departed, bringing joy to you with the touch of his hand?
Thinking that they might look at these [flowers] because of their humility despite their excellence in quality, they ask:
"O Mālatī, O Mallikā, O Jāti!"
"O Yūthikās, what was seen by you? Did he go away, generating joy for you with the touch of his hand?"
In this regard, the internal distinction between *mālatī* and *jāti* should be observed.

May the mango, priyāla, panasa, āsana, kovidāra, jambu, arka, bilva, bakula, āmra, kadamba, nīpa, and whatever other trees exist on the banks of the Yamunā for the sake of others, proclaim the path of Kṛṣṇa to us whose souls are bereft of Him.
Thinking, "May these [trees], which satisfy all living beings with their fruits and so forth, see [us]," they ask: "O mango tree," etc.
There is a distinction between the sub-species of the mango (*cūta*) and the *āmra*, as well as between the *kadamba* and the *nīpa*.
O mango trees and the others!
"And others who exist for the sake of others" means those whose very existence or birth is solely for the benefit of others;
"those on the banks of the Yamunā" means those dwelling near its shore; the meaning is "those who reside at sacred fords (tīrthas)."
May those venerable ones describe—that is, tell—the path of Kṛṣṇa, the way of Kṛṣṇa, to us who are devoid of self and whose minds are empty.
O Earth, what penance have you performed that you shine with the hairs of your body bristling from the festival of touching the feet of Keśava?
Is this birth from his foot, or from the stride of the Wide-Strider (Urukrama), or perhaps from the embrace of him in the form of the Boar?
O Kṣitikṣitī (O Earth), what austerity have you performed, you who possess a festival of the touch of Keśava’s feet— that is, for whom there is a festival through the touch of Keśava’s feet?
Why [is this so]?
"With your body-hairs bristling, you appear thrilled with horripilation; you shine forth.
Regarding this, he asks for clarification: Is this festival arising from Your feet now produced by the touch of Your foot on a single part of my body?
Or is it not merely this, but rather [arising] even before the strides of Urukrama, through the treading of all things by the foot of Trivikrama?"
Oh, or rather:
it is not only this much, but even prior to that, by the embrace of the body of the Boar.
"Therefore, you must surely have seen him; show him to me! [10.30.10]
O friend, has Acyuta come here with his beloved, bringing complete satisfaction to the eyes by displaying his limbs?
Here blows the fragrance of the jasmine garland belonging to the head of the family, which was stained by the saffron from the breasts of his beloved as she embraced his body.

Regarding the term *eṇapatnī*: according to the grammatical rule (*sūtra*) "the suffix *na* is used for the wife of a husband when connected with a sacrifice" (*patyur no yajñasaṃyoge*), the male antelopes (*eṇa*) possess the status of sacrificers through sacrifices in other lives, while the female antelope (*eṇī*) possesses the status of the sacrificer’s wife; thus, this is a praise based on what is observed. They say "even" (*api*), suggesting that the sight of the black [deer] might be possible due to its proximity to the sight of the spotted doe (*hariṇī*).
"O friend, O wife of the deer, has he indeed approached— come near—
with his beautiful limbs, such as his face, arms, and so forth?"
Regarding what was said, "together with his beloved," that is the indicator:
the fragrance of a jasmine flower garland, which has been colored by the saffron from her breasts due to contact with her body;
[this belongs] to the noble lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
A whirlwind approaches.
O trees, as Rāma’s younger brother— holding a lotus, his arm resting upon the shoulder of his beloved, and followed by swarms of bees blinded with passion for the *tulasī*—
dwells here, does he perhaps welcome you with affectionate glances as he wanders?

[*28] Seeing the trees bent by the weight of their fruit upon the shoulders of his beloved, who was affectionately leaning against his shoulder, Kṛṣṇa thought they were bowing down before him; thus, imagining the graceful movement of his gait along with his beloved, they ask: "His arm...
[etc. He is wandering here, followed and pursued by swarms of bees intoxicated by the fragrance of the *tulasī*.
Ask these creepers that have embraced the arms of the tree;
surely, touched by his fingers, they now bear horripilation, alas!
Some said: "O friends, these creepers have surely been united with Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, ask them."

"Is it not the case that union with her [the goddess] is difficult to achieve when one is already united with one's own husband? No; for even though they are embraced by the arm of their husband, the Lord of the Forest (the tree), they surely possess great fortune since they bear horripilation from being touched by his nails.
For such a manifestation of horripilation does not occur through union with one's own husband—this is the intended meaning."
Thus the cowherd girls, distressed in their search for Kṛṣṇa, repeated those words of the madman;
indeed, being absorbed in him, they imitated his various divine pastimes.

It has already been explained that they questioned [Kṛṣṇa] like madmen; now, he elaborates upon what was stated in the verse, “They then took on those various gestures of the Lord of Ramā,” by means of the word *iti*.

The phrase *unmattavacaḥ* refers to the words of the madmen, and *tā gopyaḥ* refers to those gopīs who were themselves like madwomen. They were distressed by their search for Kṛṣṇa and were extremely agitated.
They imitated her; they acted in accordance with her.
While one was acting like a *pūtana* demoness, Kṛṣṇa drank her breast; another, having acted like a child and cried out, he struck with his foot as she lay like a cart.

The imitation is elaborated by the four verses beginning with "kasyāścit"; thereafter, there is absorption into that state through four verses, and then again, imitation through one verse—this is the distinction.
She drank from the breast of the woman acting like Pūtanā (pūtanāyantī), who was behaving like Pūtanā, while she herself was acting like Kṛṣṇa.
Having made oneself like a drop, as it were, by being as small as a drop.
Acting like a Daitya, one [demon] carried off another who possessed the nature of a young black antelope;
while dragging her by the feet with the sounds of the cowherd settlement, she leaped about.
Dragging her feet along with the tinkling sounds of the small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*), she moved about in a playful dance;
the causative sense (*ṇij-artha*) is not intended here.

Having acted like a demon (*daityāyitvā*), that is, having made herself like the demon Tṛṇāvarta, she carried off another girl who was meditating upon Kṛṣṇa’s childhood (*kṛṣṇārbhabhāvanāṃ*), she who contemplates the infancy of Kṛṣṇa.
Just as those who have gone far away call out to one who follows after Kṛṣṇa,
so others praise her as she plays the flute and sports, saying, "Well done!"
"Dūragāḥ" means cows that are far away;
"yadvat" means just as; "kṛṣṇaḥ" refers to Kṛṣṇa; "tathāhūya" means having called out to that Kṛṣṇa, or alternatively, there is a reading meaning "anukurvatīm," which signifies "imitating."
"Do not fear the wind and rain; I have provided a protection for that," he said, and with one hand he held up his garment while making an effort.
Exerting herself, making an effort, she raised up her garment, the upper cloth, holding it aloft.
There, one said: "O cowherds, look at this fierce forest fire! Close your eyes quickly; I shall provide for your safety immediately."
Close [your eyes]; close them completely.
There, a certain slender woman with beautiful eyes, having tied another garland around her waist upon the mortar, covered her mouth in fear and feigned terror.
Having covered her face, which possesses beautiful eyes,
[he says] "O fair-eyed one," or "O lovely-eyed one.
This is a mockery of fear, an imitation of terror.
Thus questioning Kṛṣṇa, the creepers and trees of Vṛndāvana beheld in that forest region the footprints of the Supreme Soul.
Thus once again, in Vṛndāvana, in a certain part of the forest, in a region of the woods, the creepers and trees, questioning Kṛṣṇa,
beheld him.
Seeking her path by those various footprints, the women went ahead; seeing them closely matching the footsteps of their bride, they spoke in distress.
Well-blended and thoroughly mixed.
Whose steps are these, taken by one who has gone with the son of Nanda,
her forearm resting upon his shoulder like a female elephant with a male elephant?
She upon whose shoulder her forearm was placed—
[like] that of a female elephant (*kareṇu*).
Surely the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, has been propitiated by her,
since Govinda, being pleased, abandoned us and led her away into solitude.
One should go to a solitary place.
Oh, blessed indeed are these particles from the lotus-feet of Govinda,
which Brahmā, Śiva, and the goddess Ramā bear upon their heads for the destruction of their sins!
[*30] *Agha* means sin, offense, or the sorrow of separation. O friends,
oh, how blessed and most meritorious are the dust-particles from the lotus-feet of Govinda!
The reason for this is expressed by the words "those which" (*yān*).
The intended meaning is that even we are capable of attaining Kṛṣṇa in exactly that same way through the consecration of dust (*reṇvabhiṣeka*).
These high words of hers cause us great agitation,
for she alone, having carried off the Gopīs, enjoys the lower lip of Acyuta in secret.
[*31] *Uccaiḥ* means excessive agitation or suffering.
[*32] The reading is "he enjoys wealth" (*dhanaṃ bhuṅkte*). Others say: "of her" (*tasyāḥ*).
She is the very essence of all the gopīs.
This is the meaning: this would indeed be so if her footprints were not present; however, they cause us distress. (BhP 10.30.30)
[*33] If her footprints were not intermingled, then the service of that dust from her feet would be a means for attaining Kṛṣṇa.
But those footprints are indeed intermingled; they do not cause pain because they are mixed with the dust of her feet—the implication being that it is the dust of Kṛṣṇa’s feet [that is present].
Surely her footprints are not visible here because of the young grass shoots;
for her beloved carried his beloved away, whose well-formed soles were being pained by them.
Searching for nothing but the pure dust of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, which was unadulterated by anything else, she became even more deeply distressed upon seeing them;
this he expresses in three verses beginning with "na lakṣyante.
He lifted her, whose well-formed and delicate soles were suffering, and placed her upon his shoulder.
Here, for the sake of his beloved, the lover gathered flowers;
yet as he stepped upon them with the forepart of his foot, they saw that his entire foot was covered.
Behold their two feet, which are not fully planted on the ground because they tread upon the earth with only their toes, thereby crushing it.
Moreover, the hairdressing of a beloved woman was performed here by her lover;
and while he was braiding his beloved's hair, he must certainly have sat down right here.
Seeing the mark on her who was seated between Kṛṣṇa’s knees, they said, "It is the sign of hair-dressing.
Regarding his beloved, he must have certainly sat down while arranging those flowers into a crest, binding them in imitation of a topknot.
Yet he, delighting in the Self and finding pleasure in the Self, remained unbroken as he sported with her,
displaying to those possessed by desire both their wretchedness and the wicked nature of women.
The reading is "svātmarataḥ. The phrase beginning with "reme" (he rejoiced) is the speech of Śuka. "Ātmarataḥ" means satisfied by himself.
One who delights in the self has his own play;
he is unbroken by the amorous distractions of women. If that is so, why did he take pleasure? To this he says: "of those possessed by desire."
And she then considered herself the most excellent of all women, thinking:
"Abandoning the cowherd girls who desire him, that beloved one is approaching me."
He describes the wicked nature of women with two verses beginning with "sā ca":
she considered herself superior for the reason that, having abandoned the gopīs whose vehicle—meaning the means of their approach—was desire (kāma), she was now devoted to me.
When he had spoken thus, he said to his beloved, "Mount upon my shoulder," and then Kṛṣṇa vanished; that bride was filled with remorse.
He shows the wretchedness of those possessed by desire with the words "Thus he spoke.
He states her unbroken state with the words "And then.
The meaning is that she had vanished just as she was about to climb onto his shoulders.
"Alas, my Lord, my Beloved, my Dearest! Where are you, where are you, O mighty-armed one?
O friend, show yourself to me, your wretched maidservant."
He spoke with remorse, saying, "Alas, my Lord!"
Seeking the path of the Blessed One,
the cowherd women saw from nearby their distressed companion, who was bewildered by the separation from her beloved.
Seeking and searching for [it],
not far away, in the vicinity.
Then, entering the forest as long as the moonlight could still be discerned,
the women turned back upon perceiving that it had entered into darkness.
Then, accompanied by her as well, they entered the forest to search for Kṛṣṇa;
thereafter, they desisted from their search for Hari.
With their minds fixed on him, their speech directed toward him, their movements centered on him,
and their very selves absorbed in him, they sang only of his virtues and did not remember their own praises.
Thus, even though they had not yet reached their own homes, they did not remember them at all;
"tadātmikāḥ" means those for whom that very [object] is their self—i.e., they were absorbed in that. //BhPC_10.30.43//
Returning once more to the bank of the Kālindī, those who meditated upon Kṛṣṇa gathered together and sang of Kṛṣṇa, longing for his arrival.

However, having come to that very sandbank of the Kālindī where they had previously met with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they meditated upon and contemplated Kṛṣṇa; thus, those who longed for Kṛṣṇa’s arrival gathered together and sang only of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the first half of the tenth book of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavatamahāpurāṇa*, in the commentary known as the *Bhāvārthadīpikā*.
In the thirty-first chapter, having lost all hope, they returned once more to the riverbank;
singing only of Kṛṣṇa, they then prayed for his arrival.
The gopīs said:
By your birth, Vraja is supremely victorious; for here, Indirā dwells eternally.
O Beloved, let her be seen! Your own people, their lives surrendered to you, search for you in every direction.

[*35] In verses beginning with "jayati" (He conquers), it should be understood that generally there is a single consonant (*hal*) for the second syllable of each of the four quarters; in some quarters, there is a single consonant for the first and seventh syllables; and in certain instances, there is identity due to the phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*) established by the conventions of poets and others regarding sounds such as *śa*, *sa*, *ba*, and *va*.

[*36] In the phrase "tvayā dṛśyatām," the imperative (*loṭ*) is used in the impersonal passive sense (*bhāve*), because the verb is intransitive when the sense of instigation (*preraṇā*) is abandoned, meaning "let it be seen" or "let it become perceptible."
Alternatively, "let us be seen by you" is the imperative (loṭ) in the passive sense.
As for "he conquers": O beloved, by your birth, Vraja conquers—that is, it exists in excellence—just as it becomes superior.
Because you were born here, therefore Indirā Lakṣmī indeed takes refuge here; having adorned Vraja, she dwells within it.
While all of Vraja is thus rejoicing, your own people—the gopīs whose very lives have somehow been sustained for your sake alone—are searching for you.
Therefore, let yourself be seen; let yourself become manifest.
"Or rather, let you be seen by us;
or else, let these [beings] be seen by you as they search," [he said].

O Lord of the Gods, O Giver of Boons, is there not slaughter here for you when you strike down your own handmaid, who was given to you without price and whose eyes steal the splendor of the interior of a beautiful autumn-born lotus?
Alternatively, the construction is: "Or rather, by the very act of looking—by the bride-price of the form of their gaze—they kill even the slave-girls through abandonment.
Here, because the independent arms are the speakers, the introduction "others say" (*aparā āhuḥ*) is applied to every verse; nevertheless, the connection is now stated.

If it be asked, "What is it that they discern about me there? they say: "By that gaze"—O Lord of the gods' delight!—which robs away the splendor found within the interior, the very core, of the blossomed lotus that has arisen well in a lake during the autumn season, a lake belonging to the autumn time.
O Lord of Enjoyment, bestower of boons and desired objects, is this killing—which you are performing here in this world by slaying these priceless slave-girls—not killing?
Is killing only killing when done with a weapon; does it not also constitute killing when done with a glance?
However, it indeed exists;
therefore, the sense is that you should look [upon it] in order to restore the life-force stolen from you by my gaze.
The phrase "you should look" is to be understood as the ellipsis at the end of every sentence as appropriate.

O Ṛṣabha, we have been protected by you again and again from the danger of being submerged in poisonous waters, from predatory beasts and rākṣasas, from rain and wind, from the fire of lightning, and from the universal fear arising from the son of Vṛṣa.
Vatsāsura was the son of Vṛṣa, as in the phrase "he emerged from the mouth of a boar.
Vyomāsura was the son of Maya.
Although his life story will be told later, it should be understood that it occurred prior to the Rāsa dance.
Furthermore, they say: "Having protected us out of compassion from many deaths, why do you now send the god of love (Manmatha) with your glance to have him slain?"—beginning with "viṣa":
O best of sages (ṛṣabha), [we were saved] from destruction by poison, from water and so forth, as well as from the serpent, from the Rākṣasa Aghāsura, and from the wind during the rains.

The meaning is: "Since you have protected [the gods] from the fire of lightning, from the fall of thunderbolts, from the bull-demon Aṛṣṭa, from that son of mine [Hiraṇyakaśipu], from the sky, from everything else, and from all fears by means of the subduing of Kāliya and other deeds—why do you now neglect them?"
Indeed, you, the delighter of the cowherd girls, who perceives the inner self of all embodied beings,
having been entreated by Vikhanas for the protection of the universe, have arisen as a friend in the lineage of the Sātvatas.

[*39] Although the slaying of the demons Ariṣṭa and Vyoma was yet to happen, it is referred to as if it had already occurred because it was heard from the mouths of Garga and others, or because it serves to nourish the theme of deception.
Furthermore, with the intention that "neglecting your devotee is utterly unbecoming for one who has descended for the protection of the universe," they say: "Certainly not.
O friend, you certainly (*khalu*) are not the son of Yaśodā.

But he is the witness of the intellect of all living beings. Now, one might ask: "Is he visible? To this they reply: "Having been entreated by Brahmā, who is known as Vikhanas, for the protection of the universe, he has arisen—meaning he has appeared—in the lineage of the Sātvatas. (BhP 3.2.4)

O bull among the Vṛṣṇis, O beloved one, place upon our heads— our heads that have come to your feet out of fear of saṃsāra— that lotus-hand which bestows boons and grasps the hand of Śrī, thereby granting us fearlessness.
The reading is "śaraṇam īyuṣām" (for those who have gone for refuge).
Alternatively, some say that because it is both "lovely" (*kānta*) and "granting desires" (*kāmada*), it is by its very nature blissful and bestows what is desired.
Therefore, they say: "Please fulfill this fourfold prayer of ours, your devotees," using the four verses beginning with "viracitābhayam" (having manifested fearlessness), and so forth.
O leader of the Vṛṣṇis,

O beloved, place that lotus-foot of Yours upon my head— that foot by which fearlessness was granted to living beings who have sought refuge out of fear of worldly existence, and which bestows desires, grants boons, and holds the hand of Śrī.
O Hero who removes the suffering of the people of Vraja, whose smile destroys the pride of Your own kinswomen;
O Friend, favor us, Your maidservants, and show us Your beautiful lotus-face.
Alternatively, the construction [of the verse] is as follows: "Worship others who are servants of non-existence (the gods), and do not show us your lotus-face;
for death is certain. This is applied to the context of a lover's anger (*praṇayakopa*).
O Hero, O Dispeller of the distress of the people of Vraja,
O Friend whose smile destroys the pride— that is, the arrogance— of Your own people; please favor us, Your maidservants, and take us as Your refuge.
"This is certain:
first of all, show us the beautiful lotus-faces of the women."

O Kṛṣṇa, place upon our breasts Your lotus feet— which draw away the sins of embodied beings who bow before You, which follow the grazing cows, which are the abode of Śrī, and which rest upon the hoods of the serpent— and cut asunder the desire dwelling in our hearts.

The sense is that, just as the pride of a serpent’s venom is destroyed by the mere act of placing it upon its hoods, so too the destruction of Kandarpa (the god of love) is not difficult by the mere touch of his heart.

Without distinction, he who destroys the sins—that is, the destroyer of the evils—of all embodied beings who bow down before him, follows even the grass-eating animals out of compassion; thus, he is the abode of Fortune through his auspiciousness, and is placed upon the hoods of serpents due to his extraordinary valor.
Place Your lotus feet upon our breasts;
for what purpose?
To cut—that is, to sever—*hṛcchaya*, the desire dwelling in the heart.
O lotus-eyed hero, with your sweet voice, your charming speech, and words pleasing to the wise, satisfy us— who are fainting— with the nectar of your lips, for we are your servants.
Or rather, these very women before us are now bewildered by separation from your speech that carries out their commands;
O lotus-eyed one,
[console them] with your own sweet voice— that voice which possesses lovely words, which is pleasing to the wise, heart-pleasing, and profound.
"O you who perform our rites, these female servants of ours are fainting; revive them by nourishing them with the nectar of your lips. Thus he spoke.

Those people who bestow abundant gifts recite upon this earth your nectar-like story— which is praised by poets, which sustains the scorched, which removes impurity, which is auspicious to hear, and which is glorious and pervasive.

[*45] Or rather, those who are tormented say: "Your very words are nectar, yet it is that same nectar which kills us by way of being an inflamer [of passion]. Likewise, 'life in heat' means life as if in heated oil.
And thus, those who speak before us are great givers, yet they are great destroyers.
The verbal root is "do" in the sense of "breaking.
Therefore, the construction is: "enough with the nectar of your story.

Furthermore, they say: "O Lord, although death has indeed already arrived for us in separation from you, we have been cheated by those fortunate ones who drink the nectar of your stories"—this is expressed in the verse beginning with "tava" (of you).
Speech alone is nectar;
the reason for this is that it sustains life even when parched.
They say it surpasses the well-known nectar in that it is praised and not oppressed even by poets who are knowers of Brahman.
But the nectar to be enjoyed by the gods was treated as trivial by them;
moreover, that true nectar— which removes impurity and dispels desire and karma— is not like this.
Moreover, it is an auspiciousness to hear, bestowing auspiciousness by the mere act of hearing;
however, that [other type] depends upon its performance.
Furthermore, it is glorious and perfectly peaceful.
But that nectar of your speech is intoxicating; those people on earth who thus recite and describe it as it truly is are "givers of much," meaning they bestow life itself.
Alternatively, those on earth who recite such nectar of Your story are "givers of much," meaning they have performed many meritorious deeds in previous births.
This is what is intended: even those who merely recite the nectar of the story are exceedingly fortunate; how much more so those who behold You?
Therefore, we pray: "May You be beheld by us."
O Deceiver, Your laughter, Your loving glances, Your playful movements, and Your meditative blessings;
those secret intimacies that touch the heart—all these truly agitate my mind.
[46] Bestowing auspiciousness through mere meditation—this is a qualification of [the Buddhas] such as Prahasita.
[An objection: "Are you not already satisfied by merely hearing my discourse? What is the use of seeing me? [Response: No.
"Ours hearts are agitated by your amorous play, yet even there we find no peace," they say:
"O beloved, O deceiver, O rogue, [your] jests of secret signals! (BhP 31.10).
O Lord, O Beloved, when you set out from Vraja to tend the cattle,
our minds fall into distress, thinking that your feet, as beautiful as lotuses, must be pained by the blades of grass and thorns.
Furthermore, they say in two verses—beginning with "calasi"—how their hearts are moistened by excessive love for you, yet for what reason do you practice deceit toward them?
"O Lord, O Beloved!
When you depart from Vraja while tending the cattle, then that foot of yours, beautiful as a lotus and so tender, is [pierced] by the stones..."
"By means of ears of grain, grass, and sprouts, we suffer; our minds become clouded and reach a state of unease, thinking, 'He might be distressed.
Thus, with hearts apprehensive of your suffering, we have become such as we are. (BhPC 31.11)
O Hero, at the close of day, you repeatedly instill love in our minds by displaying a forest-lotus face covered with dark locks of hair and thickly laden with pollen.

But you, at the close of day, in the evening time, bearing a face covered by dark locks of hair— like a lotus with its petals closed by thick pollen, sprinkled with the dust of cows, and surrounded by swarms of bees— you repeatedly show that face to us and instill nothing but love in our minds.
But the sense is: "You do not grant me attachment; you are a hypocrite."

O Beloved, may Your most peaceful lotus-feet— which cause agitation even by mere remembrance, which grant the desires of those who bow before You, which are worshipped by the Lotus-born Brahmā, and which are the ornament of the earth— be meditated upon in times of distress; and may You, the destroyer of our mental anguish, place them upon our breasts.

[*48] He adorns the earth with signs such as banners and the like; therefore, they now entreat him with two verses—beginning with "praṇatakāmadam"—to act thus while abandoning all deceit: "O Adhihan! O Raman! [End of verse].

"O Lord, place Your lotus feet—worshipped by Brahmā, to be meditated upon in times of distress, which remove calamities through mere meditation, most peaceful, and most blissful even during service—for the sake of quelling our fever of desire. Thus she prayed.
O Hero, bestow upon us that nectar of your lower lip— which increases love, destroys sorrow, is perfectly kissed by the whistling flute, and causes men to forget all other passions.
[*49] "Of men" means even of males, how much more so of women;
moreover, O hero!

"Grant us that lower nectar; give it to us through the flute, which is well-kissed by the resonance and the sound. The meaning is that it is "scented with the nectar of sound. It causes men to forget other attachments—that is, it makes them forget and dissolve their desire for other pleasures, such as those of a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*). (BhP 3.14)
When you wander through the forest during the day, an instant seems like an eon to those who do not see you;
yet for those whose eyes are fixed upon your face, adorned with beautiful curls, that very moment becomes a dull obstruction to their vision.
Alternatively, there is a word-break as *ajaḍa* (not insentient).
He who cuts the eyelashes is indeed the one who brings about the absence of closing—the non-insentient knower of flavor (*rasajña*).
Or rather, let him look up intensely, being non-insentient like the cutting of the eyelashes for those who gaze upon him.
The sense is this: "But we, dull-witted as we are, with eyes covered by eyelashes, what can we see?"—thus there is suffering even in the act of seeing.

Furthermore, since we experience suffering when you are not seen for even a moment and happiness when you are seen, we have become like ascetics who have renounced all attachments; thus, even a *truṭi* or half a moment becomes like an eon (*yuga*).
In this way, the suffering of not seeing you has been described.
Furthermore, at the end of the day, for those whose eyes were somehow gazing upward at Your glorious face, O Illustrious One, Brahmā—who creates the eyelashes—was indeed dull and sluggish;
for even an interval of a single blink was unbearable, such that their vision is described as blissful. (BhPC 31.15)

O gambler, having utterly disregarded your father, sons, brothers, and kinsmen— who have come to you as your final refuge— what man would abandon those women who know your path, being deluded by your song, even in the night?
Therefore, O Acyuta,
we have come into your presence, having utterly transgressed our husbands, sons, descendants, their relatives, brothers, and kinsmen. Of what sort are you?
Those who know the ways, knowing our arrival; or those who know the movements of song; or we ourselves, who know the ways.
"O deceitful rogue, who would abandon such women—who have been enchanted by your loud singing and chanting—and who have come of their own accord at night?
The meaning is: no one at all."

Beholding You— the abode of Śrī, whose secret intimacies give rise to love within the heart, whose face is radiant with smiles, whose glances are full of affection, and whose chest is broad— my mind repeatedly becomes bewildered by intense longing.
In which [place] there was a secret conversation; the absence of the *aluk* compound here is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). In which [place] there was a smiling face.
Where there is gazing with love,
excessive longing arises;
or else, "spṛhā" is derived from the root *spr̥h* in the sense of the action (bhāve) by adding the suffix *kvip*, and thus takes the third case.
The meaning is that the mind becomes deluded upon seeing [the Lord] with excessive longing;
"atispṛham" is the reading found in the Citsukha commentary.

Therefore, with the intention that you alone should provide the medical treatment for the heart-disease of ours—which was caused by our previous sight of you—now that we have been abandoned by you, they speak in two verses beginning with "rahasi."
Beholding Your abode of splendor and Your vast, expansive chest, an intense longing arises;
likewise, my mind is repeatedly bewildered.
O dear one, Your manifestation as the dweller of Vraja and the forest is the destroyer of sins and is sufficient for the auspiciousness of the entire world;
yet, please grant even a little of that which is the eradicator of the heart-pain of Your own kin, whose souls long for You.

[53] For the inhabitants of Vraja and the forest-dwellers alike, as well as for yourself, Your manifestation—the clear appearance of You who destroys the sins (*vṛjina*) of all those dwelling in Vraja and the forest without distinction—is the dispeller of suffering; thus You are the auspiciousness of the universe and the embodiment of all auspiciousness.
Therefore, abandon—release even the slightest bit—from us whose souls long for You and whose minds have ascended to the longing for You.
"Without acting out of wretchedness, give me these things.
What are they?
That which is the most secret medicine for curing the heart-diseases of one's kin—that which destroys and turns them away—you alone are that, O Vetasa; such is the hidden intention.

O beloved, that lotus-foot of yours, so well-formed, which we place slowly upon our rough breasts out of fear—it is with that very foot that you wander through the forest; does it not perhaps ache? Our minds, devoted to your life, are wandering in distress.
Overcome by excessive love, they said while weeping:
"O beloved, that delicate lotus-foot of yours which we would place and hold gently upon our hard breasts, fearing it might be bruised—
yet you wander through the forest with it."

In the reading "nayasi" (you lead), it means you lead—whether cattle, or someone else, or even yourself—to that place. Therefore, how is it that your lotus-foot does not suffer pain from things such as *kūrpa* (thorns) or other small stones?
How indeed could it not suffer? Thus, the intellect of us whose very life (*āyuḥ*) is dependent on you wanders and becomes bewildered. (BhP 31.19)
[*54] *Dadhīmahi* means "we should strive to maintain. The suffix *liṅ* is used here according to the rule: "The *kṛtya* and *tṛc* suffixes are also used in the sense of fitness (*arhe*).
[*55] Regarding the term *bhavadāyuṣām*:
And thus also begins [the verse] with "tvayi dhṛtāsavaḥ" (with their life-breaths held in you).
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the commentary *Bhāvārthadīpikā* on the first half of the tenth book of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
In the thirty-second [chapter], Hari, whose heart is moistened by the lamentations of separation, [speaks].
Manifesting there, he consoled those cowherd girls, honoring them.
This son of Nanda has arisen, forever delighting the cowherd girls whose minds are overwhelmed by the surging waves of the nectar of his own love. // 2 //
Thus the cowherd women, O King, longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa, sang aloud and lamented in various ways, weeping with melodious voices.

"Thus they were to be hidden," meaning from that point onward; "in many ways" means in various manners; those who possessed an intense longing and great desire for the sight of Kṛṣṇa, crying out in beautiful voices at the top of their lungs.
To them appeared Śauri, his lotus-like face smiling,
wearing yellow garments and garlands, the manifest destroyer of the god of love himself.
The meaning is that he is the manifest destroyer of Manmatha; that is to say, he is the manifest deluder even of Kāma, the desire who has arisen in the mind of the world-deluder.
Beholding their beloved returned, all those women, their eyes blossoming with joy,
rose up simultaneously like slender bodies returning to life.
The limbs are the hands, feet, and so forth.
A certain slender woman took the chewed betel with her joined palms; another, tormented by love, placed his lotus-feet upon her breasts.
With the two hands joined together in the añjali gesture.
Knitting her brow and overwhelmed by the intensity of her passion,
she glared as if striking him with side-long glances, her lips bitten.
Knitting her eyebrows and arching them with a surge of passion— the intensity of a lover’s anger— she,
overwhelmed and helpless, bit her lower lip and gazed at him as if striking him with the reproaches of her sidelong glances.
Delighting in that lotus-face with her unblinking eyes, she was not satiated even though she had drunk it in, just as the virtuous are never satiated by his feet.
[56] "The virtuous are devoted to service and devotion"—this is the illustration regarding the absence of satiety.
Even though she had drunk [him in] with her unblinking eyes—that is, even though she had seen him perfectly—she did not reach satisfaction as she enjoyed him again and again. (BhP 10.32.7)
A certain woman, having fixed him within her heart through the aperture of her eyes and closing them,
stood embracing him with her limbs bristling with joy, immersed in bliss like a yogi.
[*57] "Like a yogi" is an illustration for the internal manifestation; the meaning is "having taken it to the heart," that is, having brought it into the heart. //BhPC_10,32.8//
All of them, finding supreme bliss in the festival of beholding Keśava,
abandoned the fever born of separation, just as people do upon finding a wise counselor.

Just as people seeking liberation reach the wise Lord, or as worldly beings reach a wise knower of Brahman, or as individual souls in the states of Viśva and Taijasa reach the wise state of deep sleep; // BhPC 10.32.9 //
[*58] "Sauṣuptam" means the witness of deep sleep (*suṣupti-sākṣin*).
Surrounded by those [goddesses] whose sorrows had been dispelled, the Blessed Lord Acyuta shone forth exceedingly,
my dear, like the Puruṣa surrounded by his powers (*śakti*).

Just as the Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, shines forth more intensely through His powers such as *sattva* and the rest; or as the practitioner (*upāsaka*), the Puruṣa, shines through knowledge, strength, heroism, and so on; or as the latent Puruṣa, enveloped by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*), shines forth more intensely—so it is here.
Taking them with him, the Lord went down to the sandy bank of the Kālindī,
where the breeze was made fragrant by blossoming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers and by bees.
Having entered and taken possession [of it], that place where bees were present because of the breeze made fragrant by blossoming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers. //BhPC_10,32.11//
Auspicious, with the darkness of its faults dispelled by the mass of rays from the autumn moon,
the river Kṛṣṇā has soft sands caressed by her trembling hands.
That [place] in which the darkness of the night—the gloom born of defects—has been destroyed by the masses, the multitudes, of the rays of the autumn moon;
therefore, it is auspicious and brings happiness.
It is one in which soft sands are strewn and covered by tremulous waves in the form of hands.
The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: having taken up such a sandbank and enjoyed it, he, surrounded by them, shone even more brilliantly.
With the pain of their hearts shaken away by the joy of seeing him, they reached the fulfillment of their desires as the Vedas reach their end;
with their own upper garments marked by the saffron from her breasts, they offered a seat to their own kinsman.
And they reached the end of their desires; they became fulfilled, just as the Vedic scriptures [do].

This is the meaning: just as in the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), the Vedic scriptures, not perceiving the Supreme Lord, become as if incomplete due to their attachment to various specific desires.

In the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍa), however, it is said that having seen the Supreme Lord, they become filled with His bliss and abandon the pursuit of desires; likewise, even though their desires were already fulfilled, they worshipped Him out of love. This is expressed by the word "svaiḥ" (by their own [songs]). They "acīkapan," meaning they composed [hymns].
To the inner controller, who is the kinsman of the self.

Seated there, that Lord, whose throne was fashioned within the hearts of the masters of yoga, shone forth as he entered the assembly of the gopīs; honored by them, he bore a form that was the singular abode of the splendor of the three worlds.
[*60] "hṛdikalpitāsanaḥ" is an *aluk* compound (where the case-ending is not elided). [*61] Honored—that is, treated with hospitality—by means of betel, playful smiles, and so forth;
being thus esteemed by the assembly of gopīs as he came from among them, he shone, that is, he was resplendent.
Bearing—that is, displaying—that body which is the sole abode and locus of all the fortune and splendor found within the three worlds.
Having honored that inflamer of passion with playful, smiling glances and the arching of their brows,
and having offered praise by touching his feet and hands as they sat upon his lap, they spoke somewhat indignantly.
[*62] They spoke—that which is about to be stated; the word "asked" (*papracchuḥ*) is to be supplied as the sense.

They were characterized by their eyebrows, which possessed a playful grace (*vilāsa*) through a glance full of sudden charm (*sahāsa-līlā-īkṣaṇa*). [This was done] by means of touching—that is, by massaging. //BhPC_10,32.15//
The gopīs said:
"One person reciprocates with those who worship him; another does the opposite of this;
and yet another worships neither. O noble sir, please explain this to us clearly."
The reading is: “[Others do not resort to either].

In this regard, those with hidden intentions, desiring to attribute ingratitude to the Blessed One by means of his own words, ask as if inquiring about worldly affairs: “They resort [to them],” meaning “sentient beings who resort [to them].”
"Anu" means immediately following. Some worship in accordance with that [previous] devotion; others do so in the opposite manner.
Those who do not worship them out of regard for those [who do] are nevertheless worshipped by them; others, however, are worshipped by neither. //BhPC_10.32.16//
[64] Regarding those who serve both and those who serve neither,
the Blessed One said:
"Those friends who serve one another are indeed solely intent on their own self-interest."
In that regard, there is neither friendship nor dharma; for that is solely for the sake of one's own interest and not otherwise.
[*65] "Not otherwise for the sake of another" is the meaning.
Having understood the intention, he says the reply: "Mutually.
O friends, those who associate with one another through a system of favor and counter-favor do not serve another; rather, they serve only themselves.
Why?
Because those whose exertion is directed solely toward their own self-interest have no affection for others; therefore, there is no happiness therein.
And the Dharma is not like the distribution of cattle, buffaloes, and so forth according to visible worldly purposes; such is the meaning.
[66] Toward their own interest, that is, toward their own visible fruit;
[67] they possess no genuine affection because it consists of deceit. Those who indeed show favor even to one who does not return it are compassionate, like fathers.
In this [teaching], the Dharma is free from censure, and there is friendliness toward those of the middle way.
"Without reproach" means "without contradiction.
This is also a qualification of friendliness (*sauhṛda*).
As for those who favor one who does not favor them, they are of two kinds.
They are compassionate and affectionate;
however, in that regard, they desire the Dharma in due order, as he says: "They honor those who do not honor."
Even those who worship them do not truly worship; how much less so those who do not?
For they delight only in themselves, their desires are already fulfilled, they are ungrateful, and they betray their teachers.
Regarding the answer to the third question, "even for one who partakes [of this]," the meaning is as follows: those are of four kinds;
some are those who delight in the self and whose vision is turned away [from external objects].
Some have their desires fulfilled; though they perceive sense objects, they are devoid of the wish for enjoyment because their desires are already full.

Others are ungrateful fools, while others are exceedingly cruel betrayers of their gurus—so called because, according to the maxim "he who nourishes is a father," one who provides assistance is equal to a guru, and they act with malice toward such a person. 10.32.19.
But I, my friends, do not devote myself even to beings who devote themselves to me, for the sake of following their ways;
just as a poor man, when his newly acquired wealth is lost, remains absorbed in its concern and perceives nothing else.
There, considering herself to have reached the very limit [of her beauty], she saw those women with their faces covered by secret smiles and their eyes narrowed; seeing them, she said, "Not I.
"O friends, I am not any one among them."
But he is supremely compassionate and a supreme friend.
How so?
It is not that I do not love them; rather, it is for the sake of their continued devotion and for the purpose of engaging them in uninterrupted meditation that I do not manifest myself to them.
He states this with an illustration, beginning with "yathā" (just as):
he is "nibhṛta," meaning filled or pervaded by the very thought of that wealth; that is to say, he is completely occupied by it.
He does not experience anything else, such as hunger, thirst, or the like.

Thus, O beloved women, for the sake of following me—who have renounced the world, the Vedas, and my own kinsmen for your sake—I remained hidden from your sight; you ought not to feel resentment toward that which was done for your own pleasure.

Thus, for you who have abandoned the world, the Vedas, and your own kin for my sake— having abandoned the world by disregarding what is proper or improper, the Vedas by disregarding dharma and adharma, and your own kin by renouncing affection— to you who were enjoying yourselves in my absence so that I was out of sight, [my disappearance] occurred even while you were merely listening to my loving conversations.
It remains in a state of invisibility.
Therefore, O weak ones, O beloveds, you ought not— indeed, you are not fit— to find fault with me by looking upon me with malice.

Alternatively, the two *mā*s are used for negation; nevertheless, [the meaning is]: "You ought not (*mā*) to be envious of me, who am characterized by suffering. Rather, because I have inflicted suffering upon you, it is indeed appropriate (*athaiva*).

Even with the lifespan of the gods, I would not be able to repay your own good deeds, you who are joined to the blameless; therefore, let that [debt] be discharged toward you through my virtuous conduct, for you have severed those difficult-to-break chains of the household life and have devoted yourselves to me.
Alternatively, there is the reading "śṛṅkhalām.
Let this be; however, he says "no" to indicate, "Listen rather to the ultimate truth":
O wise ones, even with my long life, I am not able—that is, I cannot—perform a good deed or a service in return for you, whose union is faultless and perfectly joined.
How so?
Those women who are difficult to overcome and undecaying—the chains of the household—having severed them completely and cut them away without remainder, do not cling to me;
for my mind, being filled with affection for many, is not fixed on any one alone.
Therefore, by your own virtuous deed—that is, by your good conduct—let that [debt] of yours be repaid; let it be counteracted.
The meaning is: my freedom from debt toward you is through your very goodness of character alone, and not through any reciprocal service rendered by me.
[*71] Or rather, because he is wise (*budha*) and skilled in calculation, even with that infinite lifespan [it would not suffice].
