Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the *Bhāvārthadīpikā* commentary on the first half of the tenth book of the glorious *Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
**32** Then, in the thirty-third [chapter], Hari, situated in the midst of the circle of cowherd women—
He delighted those beloved women with sports in lotus ponds and groves.
Śrī Śuka said: Having thus heard these most beautiful words of the Blessed One, the gopīs—
whose blessings were fulfilled by his very limbs— abandoned the fever born of separation.
Exquisite and captivating;
O King, at that time,
they were those whose blessings were augmented— that is, made abundant— by the limbs of that Blessed One, by his body, or by his members such as hands and feet.
Or rather, he whose blessings were accumulated by the limbs of those gopīs—
there Govinda began the rāsa dance with his devoted followers,
accompanied by those jewels among women who were full of joy and joined their arms around one another.
The *rāsakrīḍā*—the sport known as the *rāsa*, which is a particular kind of dance accompanied by many female dancers—is that play;
[He performed it] together with those whose arms were mutually bound and interlaced.
[74] “When actors have their necks clasped by one another, and the dancers have taken hold of each other’s hands, there occurs a *rāsa*, which is a dance performed in a circular formation.”
Thus is the definition of the *rāsa*.
The *rāsa* festival commenced, adorned by the circle of *gopīs*,
with Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, in the midst of them, [uniting] two by two.
Having entered, he placed the women, who had been seized, by their necks close to himself.
[75] It has proceeded by means of a dark sign;
or rather, the causative sense is implied within the root:
the meaning is that it has proceeded correctly by means of the dark [sign].
He demonstrates that association through performance with one and a half verses, beginning with the four syllables "rāsotsave.
He has entered between each pair of those [gopīs] who are situated in the form of a circle, and by him alone they are grasped by the neck and embraced on both sides.
In what manner? By him... [who is... (as follows).
The meaning is that he entered between each pair [of women] so that every woman might think, "He has embraced me alone, who am near him.
Now, one might ask: how can a single person enter in such a way?
Or, even if he were present near everyone, why would they have the conceit that he was near only themselves? To this, it is said: "by the Lord of Yoga" (yogeśvareṇa).
The meaning is: "by means of inconceivable power."
One might think that the sky was so crowded with hundreds of celestial palaces that the hearts of the gods and their wives were captivated by intense longing.
At that very moment, the sky became crowded and filled with hundreds of celestial chariots belonging to the gods and their wives, whose minds were pervaded by eagerness.
Then the drums resounded, showers of flowers fell,
and the lords of the Gandharvas, together with their wives, sang that stainless fame.
Thus they sang of that stainless, pure fame of the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
In the circle of the rāsa dance, there arose a tumultuous sound from the bracelets, anklets, and tiny bells of the women together with their beloveds.
Of those together with their beloveds and accompanied by Kṛṣṇa;
tumultuous means crowded.
There, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, shone exceedingly with them,
like a great emerald in the midst of golden jewels.
Like a great emerald among golden gems, He shone amidst those women of golden complexion who were embracing Him;
or, with the intention of referring to the eyes of the gopīs, the singular number is used even without the repetition of the middle word.
With the placement of their feet, the shaking of their arms, smiling glances, the play of their eyebrows,

waists that seemed to break under the weight, moving breasts and garments, earrings swaying against their cheeks, perspiring faces, and the loosening of the knots of their braided hair and waist-bands— such were the young wives of Kṛṣṇa.
Singing his praises, they shone like flashes of lightning within a circle of clouds.
Just as he shone with them, so too did they shine with him; thus he says:
"By the placement of his feet," and "by the shaking of his arms"—that is, by the movements of his hands—and "by the waists being bent and the breasts and garments swaying."
With cheeks trembling from the swaying of their earrings,
their faces perspiring— meaning those whose faces were shedding sweat—
and with firm knots in their braided hair and waist-bands.
Alternatively, "without knots" (agranthayaḥ) in those [men] and those [women] means having loose knots;
therein Kṛṣṇa, who possesses manifold forms, is like a circle of clouds.
These [emotions] are of many kinds; as is appropriate, one should understand that perspiration is like lightning, coldness is like frost, and song is like thunder.
Dancing with sweet voices and fond of pleasure, they sang loudly, delighted by the touch of Kṛṣṇa; by their song, this entire world was pervaded.
[*76] Regarding "nṛtyamānāḥ" (dancing): even at the time of dancing, there is singing; the suffix *śānac* is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).
Alternatively, it is the suffix *auśānac* used in the sense of habituality (*tācchīlya*).
Or else, it refers to those for whom honor (*mānaḥ*) was performed by Kṛṣṇa through his dancing.
Dancing means they were performing a dance;
"sweet-voiced" means their throats were colored with various hues;
"delighted by the touch of Kṛṣṇa" means they were gladdened by his contact.
This is the universe.
One woman sang the *svarajātis* unmixed [with the *mūrchanās*] along with Mukunda;
being pleased, he honored her, saying "Well done! Well done!
He sang that very same melody as a fixed refrain (*dhruva*) for her and bestowed great honor upon her.

Together with Mukunda, she—being delighted and honored by Him—raised her own musical scales (*svarajāti*), which consist of the melodic progressions of the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*; these were unmixed and unconfused with those raised by Kṛṣṇa. Having made the *dhruva*—the specific rhythmic measure (*tāla*) so named—the very basis for raising those scales, she raised them, that is, she performed them.
One woman, exhausted from the *rāsa* dance, grasped with her arm the shoulder of the mace-wielder standing at her side, her bracelets and jasmine flowers slipping loose.

Thus, he describes the conduct of those women who were honored by Śrī Kṛṣṇa through dancing, singing, and so forth—a conduct characterized by the play of extreme affection—beginning with the words "A certain one" (*kācit*).
She was one whose bracelets and jasmine garlands were loosening. (BhP 10.33.11)
There, having smelled Kṛṣṇa’s arm— resting on one shoulder, fragrant with blue lotuses, and anointed with sandalwood paste— he kissed it, his hair standing on end with joy.
That arm of his which possessed the fragrance of a blue lotus.
To one woman who was touching cheek to cheek, her own cheek adorned with the luster of earrings tossed about in dancing, he gave a piece of chewed betel.
[She is one] who joins—meaning brings together—her own cheek (gaṇḍa), which is adorned by the luster (tviṣ) of two earrings that are tossed about and flickering due to her dancing (nāṭya).

[The compound is analyzed as follows: "nṛtyena vikṣipte" means tossed about by dancing; "cañcale kuṇḍale" means the two flickering earrings; and "svābhāvikī gaṇḍatviṭ ca" means the natural luster of the cheek. The combination of these is "tviṣam," and she is "maṇḍitam" [adorned] by that. [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied according to the rule: "dvandvāc cudaṣahāntāt."
One woman, dancing and singing with her anklets and girdle tinkling,
stood by Śiva’s side and, exhausted, placed his lotus-hand upon her breast.
She is one whose anklets and girdle are tinkling.
Having obtained Acyuta, the beloved of Śrī and their own exclusive lover,
the gopīs embraced his neck with their arms and wandered about singing of him.
In this way, other gopīs also sported with various amorous diversions as they pleased; thus he says: "The gopīs... (BhP 10.33.15).

In the cowherd settlement where bees sang, the cowherd girls danced together with the Blessed One; their faces were beautiful with perspiration on cheeks adorned by ear-lotuses and locks of hair, and they accompanied the music of the sounds from their bracelets and anklets as garlands fell from their own hair.

There, while the musicians, singers, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and others were bewildered by the onset of aesthetic rapture (*rasāveśa*), He displayed yet another perfection of musical instruments and the like, and described the flurry of the *rāsa* dance: "With ear-lotuses..."—meaning those whose faces possessed beauty and splendor through ear-lotuses, locks of hair curling at the temples, and cheeks adorned with curls, as well as through perspiration;
"ghoṣas" refers to small bells.
With the sounds of bracelets and anklets, and with musical instruments and cymbals, they were those from whose hair garlands had slipped;
by this, it is suggested that their hair, delighted by the rhythm of the beat, seemed to perform a rain of flowers at his feet accompanied by a shaking of the head.
They danced together with the Blessed One.
Where?
In that assembly for the rāsa dance, where the bees themselves were the singers.

Thus the Lord of Ramā took delight with the beauties of Vraja through embraces, the touch of their hands, affectionate glances, unrestrained amorous play, and laughter— just as a child delights in the playful movements of his own reflection.

Just as the gopīs sported with the Blessed One through various amorous dalliances, so too the Blessed One took delight with them through His own playful charms; thus he says, "In this way. An illustration for His taking pleasure while remaining unassailed by their charms is given: "Just as a child," meaning like one whose play consists of amorous dalliance with His own reflections.

By this it is shown that He took His own skill in all arts, as well as His fragrance, beauty, sweetness, and so forth, and infused them into them, and sported with them just as a child plays with his own reflections.

O best of the Kurus, the women of Vraja— whose senses were agitated by the joy of contact with His limbs, and whose garlands and ornaments had become disarrayed— were not at all able to straighten their hair, their silken garments, or their bodices.

They became overwhelmed by the Lord’s playful charms; thus he says: "By his limbs," etc. By the contact with his body, their senses—which were agitated and rendered powerless by that intense joy—became such that they were no longer able (*alam*), nor capable, to immediately restore their loosened hair and other [ornaments] as they had been before.
Those whose garlands and ornaments have fallen away.
[*78] Beholding the *Kṛṣṇavikrīḍita* performed with direct and continuous connection, the women of the sky-dwellers were bewildered;
afflicted by desire, and the Moon, together with his attendants, was struck with amazement.

It is not only those [planets] whose faculties were agitated, but even the goddesses as well; thus he says, "The Play of Kṛṣṇa" and "Furthermore, by Śaśāṅka. By this it is indicated: because Śaśāṅka was struck with wonder, he forgot the path; consequently, all the planets that preceded him remained right where they were. And so, during those exceedingly long nights, [they stayed] at their ease.
They dwelt there. //BhPC_10,33.19//
Having made himself as many-fold as there were cowherd women,
the Blessed One, though delighting in his own self, sported with them in play.
And what does "having done what" mean?
The intended sense is this: “O Kātyāyanī, O Great Māyā, O Great Yoginī, O Sovereign Lady!
O Goddess, make the son of Nandagopa my husband; salutations to you!”

Thus, because each of them had made such a request, and because the Blessed One had likewise promised, saying, "O powerful ones, go to Vraja; having been perfected by me, you shall enjoy these nights," he assumed as many bodies as there were [gopīs] and took his pleasure with them.
*Yāvatīr yāvatyaḥ* means "as many as there were."
To their faces, which were exhausted by excessive dalliance, he...
The compassionate one, with his hand of most peaceful touch, lovingly wiped away the blood from his body.
The reading is “tāsāṃ rativihāreṇa. He speaks of the excellence of compassion with the word “tāsām. (BhPC 10.33.21)

The cowherd women, their pride sustained by His smile and glance— the beauty of whose cheeks was illuminated by the luster of his shimmering golden earrings and locks of hair— sang of the Lord’s meritorious deeds, their hearts overflowing with joy at the touch of His fingernails.
Then he describes the conduct of the gopīs who were exceedingly joyful: "The gopīs," it says.

With their cheeks graced by the luster of shimmering golden earrings and locks of hair, and by their well-composed glances which acted like nectar (*sudhita*) accompanied by smiles, they offered honor (*māna*) to their lord, Kṛṣṇa, the preeminent one (*ṛṣabha*), and sang of his deeds.
Those women who experience joy through the touch of his kararuhas—that is, his nails.

Accompanied by them, whose garlands were crushed by contact with his limbs and who were stained with the saffron from their breasts, he entered the water to dispel his fatigue, followed by the Gandharva maidens, like a weary lordly elephant who has broken through a dike and is pursued by female elephants.

[*82] The reading is "svakucakuṅkuma. Now he describes the water-sport with the words "tābhiḥ" (by them). By the contact of their limbs, the garland was rubbed—that is, crushed—and for that very reason, it was stained by the saffron from their breasts.

Accompanied by his relatives, who were like Gandharva kings singing with the melodies of the Gandharvas, Kṛṣṇa entered the water; he was followed by them as they pursued him, having broken the embankments,
torn up the dikes, and himself transcended the boundaries of worldly and Vedic law.
There, being splashed with water by young women who gazed at him with love and laughed from here and there,
and being praised by the denizens of celestial chariots raining down flowers, he, possessing the grace of a lordly elephant, took delight there in his own natural joy.
There is also a reading: "sprinkled with love" (*premṇokṣitaḥ*).
He delights in the self (*svaratiḥ* = *ātmārāmaḥ*), or else he is one whose delight (*ratiḥ*) is in those various [objects].
Or rather, what is his own unique delight? It is water-sports;
for even though he is one who finds delight in the Self (svarati), he delights here in this circle of gopīs or in the water.
And then, in the grove of Kṛṣṇa, where the quarters were filled with breezes scented by the flowers of water and land,
he moved about surrounded by throngs of female bees like a rutting elephant accompanied by herds of female elephants.
Having shown the sports on land and in water, he now shows the forest sports with the words "Then" (*tataś ca*).
[The phrase] refers to that grove which is frequented by a breeze carrying the fragrance of flowers born both in water and on land;
or else, it refers to that grove in which the quarters of the sky and the banks—the dry land—are present.
He was surrounded by throngs of bumblebees and of young women.

Thus, that Satyakāma, accompanied by a multitude of devoted women, enjoyed all those nights illuminated by the rays of the moon— nights which were the very essence of the aesthetic flavor found in autumnal poetry and tales, having internalized within himself the delights of love.
He concludes the account of the *rāsakrīḍā* with the word "evam" (thus):
That Kṛṣṇa, whose resolve is ever true, spent all such nights while remaining in the midst of the assembly of devoted women.
These nights were the very substratum for those aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) that arise in autumn and are described in poetic works.
Alternatively, the accusative case in "niśā" (nights) denotes continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
Thus, it means that he cultivated those stories well-known in poetic works which are the locus of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) in autumn.
Even so, this is a statement of his victory over desire: that the seminal fluid (*saurataś caramadhātuḥ*), though confined within his own self, did not leak out.

[*85] He indulged in and recounted as many autumnal poetic tales as could possibly be described by poets from all lands and times during the autumn season. O Brahmin, how could he— who was the speaker, the creator, and the protector of the bridges of Dharma— act in opposition to it by violating the wives of others?
"Pratīpam" means contrary or adverse dharma;
"ācaran" means he performed it.
And this was not merely an unrighteous act like the eating of *kalañja* and so forth, but rather a great act of violence; thus he says: "the violation of another's wife."
O observer of noble vows, what was the intention of the Lord of the Yādavas when he performed that which is indeed loathsome? Cut through this doubt of ours.

If it is argued that "this is not unrighteousness for one whose desires are fulfilled," [the author] asks—by what intention did he perform the censurable act?—"if this is so, because of the absence of desire, [he is called] 'one whose desires are fulfilled'. (BhPC 10.33.29)
Śrī Śuka said:
A transgression of dharma and even acts of violence seen in powerful lords do not constitute a fault, just as fire, which consumes all things, is not at fault.
[*86] Regarding the lords (*īśvara*), who are free from dependence on karma and other such factors;
[*87] just as the fact that fire consumes all things does not imply its impurity— so too,

in order to resolve [this objection] regarding the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic, he states the general conduct of great beings, beginning with the words "transgression of dharma" (*dharmavyatikrama*).
And acts of rashness are seen in the case of Prajāpati, Indra, Soma, Viśvāmitra, and others;
yet such acts do not result in fault for those who possess such spiritual power (*tejasvin*).
One who lacks mastery should never perform this even in thought;
by practicing it out of delusion, one perishes, just as Rudra did when consuming the ocean-born poison.
In that case, fearing that others might also act according to the principle that "whatever a superior person practices," he says: "This is not so.
One who is not the Lord (anīśvara) is dependent on the body and other such factors; just as one distinct from Rudra, while practicing or consuming poison, [is not the Lord].
The word of the lords is true, and their conduct is likewise in some instances;
a wise person should practice that which is consistent with their own words.
How, then, is right conduct (sadācāra) authoritative? To this he says: "Of the lords" (īśvarāṇām). Their word is true; therefore, one should indeed practice what they have spoken.
However, in some cases, established custom is indeed true;
therefore, one should practice whatever is consistent with one's own word and whatever is consistent and non-contradictory with their word.
"O Lord, for those who are free from egoism, there is no personal interest served by their practice of wholesome deeds here, nor is there any misfortune resulting from the opposite."
If that is so, one might ask, why do they too commit such a rash act? To this he replies with the words "by virtue of their merit" (*kuśala*).
The meaning is that their only task is the mere exhaustion of the karma already set in motion (*prārabdhakarman*), and nothing else.
Furthermore, for all sentient beings— whether animals, humans, or gods—
as well as for the rulers and those subject to their rule, what is the sequence of wholesome and unwholesome [karma]?
[*88] When even for those individual souls (*jīva*) who are subject to control, who are governed by a Lord, and who are devoid of egoism, no connection with wholesome or unwholesome [karma] exists,

then what need is there to say that for the Lord and Controller of all beings— whether in the form of animals or otherwise— no connection with the wholesome or unwholesome exists? This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) with the word "does not exist" (*na vidyate*) from the preceding verse.
He states the subject at hand: "What need is there to say more?
(kim uta). The meaning is: what further need is there to state that the sequence of wholesome and unwholesome [actions] does not exist?

Even sages, satisfied by serving the pollen of his lotus feet and having shaken off all bonds of karma through the power of yoga, wander at will yet are not bound; for him who assumes a body by his own will, how could there be any bondage?

This very point is clarified: those who are satisfied by the service of the pollen of His lotus feet—or, alternatively, those whose service is directed toward the pollen of His lotus feet and who are likewise satisfied—these are the devotees (*bhaktas*).
Similarly, the wise (*jñānins*) are not bound; that is, they have not fallen into bondage.
He who moves within all embodied beings—the Gopīs, their husbands, and everyone else—is the Overseer; here, through his play, he assumes a body.
Having previously set aside the objection regarding the gopīs being the wives of others by accepting that premise,
he now states "Of the gopīs" to show that for the Blessed Lord, the inner controller of all, there is no such thing as the pursuit of another's wife.
He who moves within as the presiding witness of the intellect and other faculties, he alone, through his divine play, assumes a body.
But he is not like us and others, such that there would be any fault.
Having assumed a human body for the sake of favoring living beings,
he engages in such sports that, upon hearing of them, one may become intent upon that [liberation].
The reading is "of those who are devoted" (*bhaktānām*).
The reading is "having remembered" (*smṛtvā*).
Now, if this is so, one might ask: how can there be activity on the part of one whose desires are fulfilled toward that which is censured? To this he says: "for the sake of favoring" (*anugrahāya*).
The meaning is: "so as to make even those who are extremely outward-looking, whose minds are drawn away by the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), [devoted] to themselves and others."
Indeed, the inhabitants of Vraja did not feel resentment toward Kṛṣṇa, for they were deluded by his illusory power;
each considered his own wife to be standing right by his side.

"Now, surely others of different conduct also say that their own actions are exactly like this"; to that he replies with the words "without envy. The sense is that those who act in such a manner when they lack such sovereign power should be known as sinful.
When the night of Brahmā had passed, the cowherd women, beloved of the Blessed One and approved by Vāsudeva, returned to their own homes against their will.
[*91] To those for whom the Blessed One is dear, or who are dear to the Blessed One;
when the Brahma-night has returned, that is, when the Brahma-muhūrta has arrived. //BhPC_10,33.39//
Whoever, endowed with faith, listens to or describes this playful pastime of Viṣṇu with the women of Vraja,
that wise person, having attained supreme devotion to the Blessed One, quickly casts off the disease of desire from his heart.
Regarding the Blessed One’s victory over desire through his playful dalliance with Rāsa and others, he states that the very fruit is the conquest of desire itself: "His play.
Being steadfast, one quickly casts off—that is, abandons—the heart-disease of desire. (BhPC 10.33.40)
Alternatively, the meaning is that having quickly obtained devotion as desired—that is, according to one's wish—it removes all heart-diseases such as desire and so forth in no long time.
This *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam Bhāvārthadīpikā*, based on the tenth book, was composed by Śrīdhara, who serves the illustrious Paramānanda. (1)
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the first half of the tenth book of the glorious Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the commentary known as the Bhāvārthadīpikā. **33**
